It is said of the action of watching. The scholiast explains: προσκοπήσας ὁ πατὴρ καὶ σημάνας ἐτάραξεν ἡμᾶς [the father, having looked out and given a signal, disturbed us].

This word was rashly introduced into the copy. Where M correctly has τάνδ᾽ ἐς ἀκρόπολιν [to this citadel], except that ἀκρόπτολιν [citadel] should be written with Porson. Some scribe substituted σκοπιάν [lookout], a word frequent in Homer, for the sake of interpretation, who no doubt had rather written this than σκοπάν [lookout]. That ἀκρόπτολιν [citadel] is correct, even if it were not evident in itself, the following words τίμιον ἕδος [honored seat] could teach. Similarly the chorus of Athenian elders in Aristophanes Lys. 263 names the citadel of Athens with a certain pride: κατὰ μὲν ἅγιον ἔχειν βρέτας, κατὰ δ᾽ ἀκρόπολιν ἐμὰν λαβεῖν [to hold the holy image, and to take my citadel].

where the scholiast: Διός σκοπὸν, τὸν Διὸς ὀφθαλμὸν τὸν πάντα σκοποῦντα. ἀλάστορα [the watcher of Zeus, the eye of Zeus that sees all things, the avenger]. Meineke Philol. vol. 20 p. 69 understands ἀλάστορα [avenger], comparing v. 414. Hermann removed the suspect particle, conjecturing πράκτορα πάνσκοπον [all-seeing avenger], to which the scholiast's interpretation τὸν πάντα ἐποπτεύσαντα [the one who has seen all] agrees.
For the corrupt words in Athen. 15 p. 667 c. the conjectures of critics have been of no avail.
